source.title: Diffusion Language Models are Super Data Learners
source.authors: Jinjie Ni; Qian Liu; Long-Xu Dou; Chao Du; Zi-Li Wang; Hang Yan; Tian-Yu Pang; M. Shieh

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out validation loss and downstream performance during repeated-data training, including cases where those trends diverge. It does not fit the power laws or compute-optimal allocations in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier scaling-law work but does not test its power-law fits, extrapolations, or compute-optimal parameter/token splits. Rows cover its own validation-loss and downstream-performance results relevant to downstream predictability and curves bending under repeated data; cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper fits no power laws and estimates no compute-optimal split. It does argue, with its own runs, that pretraining validation loss stops tracking downstream performance under heavy data repetition (Sections 3.3 and 5, Figures 2, 8 and 9). That bears on the 'with pretraining loss' part of V6. Its main result, DLM-vs-AR crossovers, is a comparison of methods, not a scaling-law test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is that under limited unique data, DLMs surpass equally sized AR models when trained for more epochs. The crossover shifts later with more or higher-quality data and earlier with larger models. The authors attribute the gain to any-order modeling, extra compute and built-in noise augmentation. They add that rising validation loss need not imply degraded downstream performance, and that DLMs also eventually overfit.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares autoregressive and masked-diffusion pretraining under repeated-data and data-constrained settings; it does not reproduce the original power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported overfitting onset varies with unique-data size and model size. The paper also says crossover timing on coding benchmarks varies with evaluation protocol, including shot setting.

fits_no_version.finding: DLMs repeated for up to 1000 epochs eventually overfit (validation loss rises). Onset comes later with more unique data and earlier with larger models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under data repetition, validation loss turns upward after a model- and data-dependent number of epochs.

record.problems: The relevant trends are largely shown in figures without extracted numeric values; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper notes that diffusion objectives optimize a variational bound rather than a normalized left-to-right likelihood, making perplexity not directly comparable.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count. Dense vs MoE is a sparsity comparison, not a test of shape.
Repeated-data training is studied, but no power-law form is fitted for it.
No fitted predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or loss. The standard non-repeated regime is not examined.
Exponents, fitting methods and parameter-count conventions are not compared.

missing.what: In the data-quality ablation, the medium-quality run achieves the lowest validation loss but does not track the benchmark ranking. The authors call validation loss 'not always a reliable comparator'.

In the 1.7B code runs, AR overfits on validation loss early while benchmark degradation is delayed. Also, DLM performance degradation comes much later than validation-loss overfitting (e.g. 0.5B tokens, 192 epochs).
missing.locator: Section 5 last paragraph; Section 6 last paragraph; Figures 1, 7

record.verdict_notes: V6 evidence is limited to the heavy-repetition regime and is mostly figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. DLM and AR losses are not directly comparable (variational bound vs exact likelihood). Shot setting changes crossover timing on code benchmarks.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss trends in parameters, tokens, or compute when other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No fits on small runs are used to predict much larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens is estimated.
Architecture variations are not tested for their effect on loss at fixed parameter count.
The study uses repeated data but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in that regime; other modalities and fine-tuning or transfer are not tested.
The study does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss; results are limited to the tested models, tasks, and training regimes.
The study reports validation-loss curves bending into overfitting under repeated data, but does not compare fitted exponents, fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.measure: Downstream task performance trend as validation loss increases
rows.value: The text states that downstream performance continues to improve despite increasing validation loss; numeric values are figure only.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the trend, but the plotted values are not provided in the extracted text. This qualifies prediction from validation loss rather than showing a fitted predictive relationship.
rows.check: Downstream accuracy keeps rising with training tokens while validation loss rises. The scale/tokens link to performance holds, but the loss link breaks. The rows give no AR model sizes, and values are figure-only.

rows.subject: 1B autoregressive model
rows.operation_detail: Tracked ground-truth and alternative-option NLLs, and their difference, on multiple-choice evaluations during pretraining.
rows.measure: Difference between ground-truth-option NLL and average alternative-option NLL (ΔNLL)
rows.baseline: At the first validation checkpoint, after 3,600 training steps, ground-truth options already had substantially lower NLL; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: The ΔNLL gap continues to widen as training proceeds, including after validation NLL begins to increase; numeric values are figure only.
rows.note: The authors interpret the widening relative-NLL gap as continuing improvement in discriminative ability despite increasing absolute NLL.
rows.check: ΔNLL between options is a mechanism measure, not task accuracy. It shows relative discrimination improving while absolute validation NLL rises. Figure-only.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V6 from this measure alone. The option-NLL gap widens despite rising absolute NLL; a growing mean gap does not establish improving task accuracy or a predictive relationship.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, Figure 9 and accompanying paragraphs; out-of-domain panel identifies Nemotron-CC training and c4-val validation.
source_check.problem: The option-NLL gap is evidence about relative discrimination, insufficient by itself to establish V6's downstream-performance effect.
